paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Green roofs are roofs covered with a layer of plants and soil. They have become increasingly common in cities looking for ways to adapt to a warmer climate. Unlike a traditional flat roof, a green roof includes a waterproof membrane, a drainage layer, a growing medium and vegetation. The idea is not new, but recent interest has been driven by rising summer temperatures and pressure on urban space. Supporters argue that a roof can do more than keep out rain: it can become a small ecosystem that provides insulation, absorbs rainwater and supports insects and birds. Some cities now treat green roofs as part of their wider strategy for cooling streets and managing water, rather than as a decorative extra.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of the main benefits is stormwater management. During heavy rain, conventional roofs send water quickly into drains, which can overflow and pollute rivers. A green roof absorbs some of this water and releases it slowly, reducing pressure on drainage systems. The plants and soil also provide insulation, keeping buildings cooler in summer and warmer in winter. In dense neighbourhoods, this can lower the demand for air conditioning. Green roofs can also create habitats for bees, butterflies and other species that struggle in paved areas, and they can give residents access to shared garden space. The combined effect is a roof that works as a small piece of infrastructure rather than a passive surface.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, green roofs are not suitable for every building. The extra weight of soil, water and plants may require structural reinforcement, especially in older buildings. Installation costs are higher than those of a conventional roof, and careful waterproofing is essential to prevent leaks. Maintenance also varies: some lightweight roofs with drought-resistant plants need little attention, while intensive roofs with trees and vegetable beds require regular watering, weeding and inspection. In dry regions, the water needed to keep plants alive can be a serious concern, and poorly designed roofs may fail within a few years. For these reasons, planners need to consider the building's age, structure and local climate before approving a project.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Policy has played an important role in the spread of green roofs. Some cities offer grants, tax reductions or planning incentives to owners who install them, and a few require new commercial buildings to include a green roof. In several European cities, green roofs have been combined with solar panels, because plants can keep the panels cooler and improve their efficiency. The results are not uniform, and the success of a project depends on local climate, building design and long-term maintenance. For cities facing heat, flooding and limited green space, however, the roof is increasingly seen as a practical piece of infrastructure rather than as an optional design feature.
